title: Incremental exposure playbook for LLM feature launch (working)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for incrementally exposing new LLM-driven product features (response shaping, tool-calling flows, and reranking) across Redwood environments. It focuses on cross-functional decision points, lightweight statistical testing for A/B, and safety/rollback mechanics that are tuned for high-cost, latency-sensitive inference.

Audience and scope:
- Primary: product managers, solutions engineers, SRE, serving runtime engineers, and applied ML.
- Scope: user-visible changes that alter model selection, prompt templates, output post-processing, or routing logic. Not included: infra-only upgrades that do not change model outputs.

Core principles (short):
- Start small, measure signal that maps to user value + safety, and prefer deterministic fallbacks over frantic manual toggles.
- Treat tokens/cost as a first-class gating dimension. A feature can be safe but uneconomical.
- Prefer staged canaries with automated rollback triggers over manual-only decisions.
- Instrument early and often: tie prompts/eval-sets to real traffic slices.

Phases (recommended pattern)
1) Bench & lab validation (local/applied-ml) — objective: model-level regressions
   - Run model on curated eval sets (prompt templates + adversarial cases).
   - Metrics: BLEU/ROUGE not enough — measure hallucination rate, instruction-following score, and business metrics mapped to golden prompts.
   - Perf: baseline P50/P95 token latency on representative sequence lengths, GPU memory profile, KV cache hit ratio.
   - Exit criteria: no >5% quality regressions on critical eval sets; perf within SLO (P95 < SLO_target).

2) Internal dogfood (company-only) — objective: integration + UX regressions
   - Enable feature behind internal flag for all Redwood employees in a single region.
   - Monitor session-level satisfaction signal (quick thumbs, support chatter), runtime errors, and token costs.
   - Keep traffic <0.5% of prod-equivalent peak to limit blast radius.

3) Constrained canary (narrow customer slice) — objective: real-world behavior + safety on production signals
   - Select 1–3 low-risk customer cohorts (non-critical workflows, small teams).
   - Traffic cap: 0.5–2% of global traffic; limit to region and plan tiers (exclude enterprise prod lanes).
   - Run for at least one full weekly cadence (to capture diurnal patterns).
   - Metrics to watch: functional correctness (eval plug-ins), latency P95 delta, error rate delta (5xx/4xx), cost per request delta, user-visible degradation signals (support tickets, CS feedback).
   - Automated canary gates: if any of these triggers, automatically fall back to stable model variant and notify owners:
       * Latency P95 increases > 2x baseline and absolute P95 > 1.5x target
       * 5xx rate increase > 0.25 percentage points or > 200% relative
       * Critical eval-set quality regression > 7%
       * Cost per request increase > 30% without matched quality uplift

4) Controlled ramp (A/B + progressive exposure) — objective: quantify uplift with statistical confidence; scale cost 
   - Typical ramp plan: 2% -> 5% -> 15% -> 40% -> 100% with observation windows between steps. Windows depend on metric volume; minimum 48 hours at the small slices, longer where variance is high.
   - Use A/B for product-impact metrics; keep feature toggles separate from model routing to allow rollback without losing experiment continuity.

Experiment design & stats notes:
- Primary metric(s): defined per feature (e.g., conversion rate on completion, accept-rate of generated suggestions, downstream click-through). Must be instrumented to event-level with model variant ID.
- Secondary metrics (safety/cost): hallucination incidents per 1k responses, P95 latency, cost per 1k requests, error rate.
- Minimum detectable effect (MDE): compute before ramp. If baseline conversion is low (<0.5%), expect need for larger samples or longer windows.
- Sequential testing: prefer group-sequential analysis or Bayesian bandit for continuous ramps. Avoid naive repeated p-value peeking.
- Multiple comparisons: if multiple metric tests or slices, adjust thresholds or use hierarchical testing.
- Decision thresholds: explicit uplift thresholds for launch (e.g., >0.7% absolute lift in high-signal metrics with 80% power) and safety bounds that cannot be overridden by product alone.

Traffic slicing guidance:
- Do not blend by geography alone. Slice by product surface, plan tier, and historical usage patterns. Example safe slices: sandbox users, small teams, API keys created in last 30 days, experimental feature flags.
- Avoid exposing new model variants to customers with heavy compliance requirements until Private deployments are vetted.

Observability checklist (must be in place before canary):
- Token-level telemetry: tokens/generated, tokens/context, average generation length per request.
- Model-level telemetry: model id, quantization profile, kernel selection, GPU instance id.
- Latency percentiles: P50, P90, P95, P99 per model + route.
- Queue metrics: request queue depth, batching delay, batch size distribution.
- Cost telemetry: estimated cost per request using current batch and token pricing model.
- Quality hooks: link each request to prompt template and golden prompt id when available.
- Alerts: automated alerts for threshold breaches and for trending regressions, not just spikes.

Runtime-specific ops (serving-runtime & infra notes):
- Pre-warm/priming: for short-lived bursts, ensure cold-start penalty is bounded — pre-provision a small pool matching canary traffic.
- KV cache priming strategy: for reranking/tool-calling flows, seed KV cache using representative prefixes to avoid early tail latency bumps.
- Batching configuration: canary should run with production batching to catch batching pathologies; simulate both low and high concurrency.
- Fallback plan: traffic router should be able to redirect to: (a) same model at lower quantization, (b) previous stable model variant, or (c) best-effort fast model with explicit degrade notice.

Runbook - immediate actions for automated gate trips:
1) Canary gate fires (automated): router toggles to fallback variant.
2) Pager on-call SRE + feature owner. Postmortem ticket auto-created (link to JIRA).
3) Observability owner posts preliminary findings: top-of-stack logs, recent deploys, sequence length distribution, batch sizes.
4) If human judgment says safe, re-enable at narrower slice for diagnosis. If not, follow rollback to 100% stable and open incident review.

Manual rollback checklist (if automated gating did not fire but human abort needed):
- Stop ramp, revert router config to 0% for the new variant.
- Disable all related feature flags and preserve logs/trace ids for later correlation.
- Capture representative failed requests (anonymize PII) and create ticket with sample prompts + model outputs.
- Notify customers in affected cohorts if visible degradation occurred.

Cost guardrails (explicit):
- Soft budget: track rolling 24h cost delta attributable to experiment. If cost delta > 15% of expected budget for the cohort AND benefit < pre-defined threshold, halt ramp.
- Hard budget: if absolute spend for the experiment > $X/day (team-set config; default $2K/day for non-enterprise features), auto-suspend.
- Token rationing: for free tiers, enforce max generation length and fallback to short-answer mode.

Safety and policy controls:
- Content safety: run new model variant through safety classifier offline + online traffic sampling. Set allowed false positive/negative budgets.
- Audit logs: every model variant activation in production must be auditable with who approved the ramp.
- Customer opt-out: provide an API param to opt a customer's workspace out of experiments.

A/B analysis templates (practical):
- Pre-registered hypothesis document per experiment (link to CONFLUENCE above).
- Data schema: event definitions, enrichment fields, attribution rules.
- A/B report template: sample size, duration, variance, power, p-values (or posterior probabilities), uplift, CI, and impact at scale.

Deployment timing & ceremony:
- Avoid large ramps before major regional cloud maintenance or holidays.
- Require cross-team sync (PM, applied-ml, runtime, SRE, CS) before each ramp step >10%.
- Post-ramp review: short 30–60 minute readout with decisions recorded in Confluence.

Owner responsibilities (concise):
- Feature owner (PM): hypothesis, acceptance criteria, comms, and customer messaging.
- Applied ML: model evals, golden prompt sets, offline regressions.
- Runtime / Infra: performance baselines, prewarm, KV cache guidance.
- Observability: dashboards and alerting.
- SRE: rollback automation and on-call.

Open questions / TODOs (working list):
- How to standardize "quality regression" across very different features (chat vs. rerank vs. embedding)? Draft an SLO-style taxonomy.
- Define default hard budget per experiment for non-enterprise customers (proposal: $2K/day).
- Add sampling hook to capture full prompts + model outputs (PII masking) for later offline labeling.
- Integrate canary decisions with rollout API so non-engineering product owners can see gate status.

Notes to self / shorthand (informal):
- If canary spike in cost but metrics good -> try quantization or lower-token fallback before abort.
- For tool-calls: instrument tool success rate + end-to-end latency separately.
- Keep rapid probe slice small but representative; sandbox-only users often have unrealistic workload.

Appendix: quick checklist before enabling canary (copyable)
- [ ] Eval-set pass (applied-ml sign-off)
- [ ] Perf baseline in lab (P95 within target)
- [ ] Dashboards created and smoke alerts set
- [ ] Cost budget assigned and circuit-breaker configured
- [ ] Customer cohorts selected and lead notified
- [ ] Rollout schedule + owner on-call calendar set

End of working draft — comments welcome.

-- Marisol (author)
